title: SLA escrow and staged-remediation flow for dedicated throughput commitments
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem statement:
Customers buying Dedicated capacity want explicit, auditable remedies when committed throughput is not met. Existing SLA language focuses on crediting but lacks: an escrow-style credit pool that vests over time, a staged remediation workflow that triggers operational actions (autoscale, burst allocations), and detailed notification/appeal windows that legal and customer success can rely on.

Goal:
Define and prototype a legally-reviewable SLA clause and an operational playbook for: 1) escrowed throughput credits (a pool that accumulates and vests during uptime), 2) staged remediation that maps degradation tiers to automated mitigations and contractual credits, and 3) observable signals and timelines (notice -> diagnosis -> remediation -> crediting) for both machine enforcement and sales/CS processes.

Scope:
- SLA contract language snippets for Sales & Legal (customer-facing) describing definitions, measurement windows, credit calculation, and appeal windows.
- Backend signals/metrics required (per-tenant p95 latency, throughput utilization vs committed throughput, error-rate per-model route).
- Staged remediation automation: preemptive autoscale / burst policy, region failover, and human escalation.
- Escrow mechanics: how credits accumulate and vest, expiration, and one-time vs recurring credits.
- Notification workflow and SLAs for internal ops and customer-facing notices (timing, content, contacts).
- Acceptance criteria and QA validation plan.

Key decisions required / trade-offs considered:
- Escrow vs immediate crediting: Escrow smooths variability and reduces dispute volume (credits vest after validation), but increases bookkeeping complexity and may delay customer compensation. We propose 50% immediate credit on validated incident, 50% escrowed and vesting over 30 days (configurable by contract tier).
- Automated remediation aggressiveness: aggressive autoscale reduces customer impact but raises cost/overprovisioning for Redwood. Proposal: define per-contract burst budget with caps; use cost-to-remediate thresholds tied to customer tier.
- Measurement window: rolling 1-hour windows for real-time automation, 30-day windows for contractual breach determination. This dual-window approach provides quick automation while protecting against false positives in contract enforcement.

Draft contract language (for Legal review) - concise clause sample:
"Dedicated Throughput Commitment": "Provider guarantees sustained throughput of X TPS for the contracted resource pool measured over a rolling 30-day window (\"Committed Throughput\"). In the event Provider fails to meet Committed Throughput, Customer will be eligible for Remediation Credits as described below. Remediation Credits are issued in two parts: Immediate Credits and Escrow Credits. Immediate Credits (up to 50% of total computed credit) will be issued upon validated incident closure. Escrow Credits (remaining portion) will be placed into an escrow pool and vest linearly over 30 days following incident validation, subject to adjustment for repeated incidents as defined in Section 3.3. Escrow Credits expire after 180 days if unused. Customer may appeal a remediation decision within 14 days of notice; appeals will be adjudicated according to the Notice & Appeal process."

Operational playbook (staged remediation):
- Tier 1 (Transient Degradation): 1-10 minute spike below target; autoscale burst policy engaged automatically. No customer credit unless repeated within 24 hours. Internal alert: paging to on-call.
- Tier 2 (Sustained Degradation): >10 minutes and <2 hours below target; automated region-level burst plus routing fallback executed. Immediate Credits applied (validated) up to 50% of computed credit. Customer notified within 2 hours with preliminary incident ID.
- Tier 3 (Severe Degradation): >2 hours below target or >20% deviation in 30-day window; regional failover & emergency capacity allocation triggered, legal and CS notified, escrow credit allocation begins. Formal post-incident report provided within 7 days.

Measurement & error budget math (example):
- Committed Throughput = 10,000 tokens/s sustained per contract.
- Measurement engine computes percentage of time rolling 30-day windows where throughput < committed threshold.
- Error budget burn rate = (total deficit tokens during window) / (Committed Throughput * window duration). Credits computed as proportional to normalized deficit and contract monthly spend, capped at X% per incident (suggested cap: 25% of monthly invoice).

Notifications & SLA timeline (customer-facing):
- T0: Detection (automated).
- T+15m: Preliminary customer notification (if Tier 2 or 3) with incident ID and mitigation in progress.
- T+2h: Validated incident notification; immediate credit estimation if applicable.
- T+7d: Post-incident RCA and escrow credit status.
- Appeal window: 14 days after validated incident notice.

Engineering requirements (signals & APIs):
- New metric streams: per-tenant committed_throughput, observed_throughput, throughput_deficit_seconds_hourly, sustained_deficit_flag.
- Audit trail: incident_id -> list of remediation actions (autoscale events, region failovers, manual overrides) with timestamps.
- Credit ledger API: escrow_pool_balance(customer), vesting_schedule(incident_id), apply_credit(customer, amount, type).
- Admin UI hooks: manual credit grant, appeal adjudication, and escalation notes.

Open questions for Legal/Finance: 
- Is linear vesting acceptable from a contractual perspective or must credits be instantaneous?
- Max cap on credits per month and per incident we should guarantee (suggest 25% monthly cap).
- Tax/accounting treatment for escrowed credits (Finance input required).

Links to artifacts / drafts:
- Draft PRD (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/DED/SLA+Escrow+and+Staged+Remediation
- Legal draft branch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/legal-sla-drafts/pull/24
- Demo dashboard prototype: https://internal.redwood.ai/dashboards/dedicated-throughput-escrow

Acceptance criteria (see list below) must be met before moving to "Done" and customer-facing language rollout.

Risks and mitigations:
- Disputes & complexity: escrow increases dispute windows; mitigate with clear audit logs and tripwires for repeated incidents.
- Cost leakage: Automated burst may spike costs; cap burst and tie to budget buckets. Provide per-customer burst budgets and opt-in aggressive remediation for lower tiers.
- Operational overhead: New playbook increases CS/Legal workload. Build tooling for auto-generated RCAs and credit statements to minimize manual work.

Next steps / immediate tasks:
- Legal: review draft clause and confirm vesting/expiration constraints (owner: legal@redwood).
- Finance: guidance on accounting and recommended monthly cap (owner: finance@redwood).
- ENG: implement credit ledger API (dependency ENG-8245) and detection metrics (dependency ENG-8361).
- PM: finalize notification templates and runbook for CS/Support.

acceptance_criteria: Measurement pipeline emits committed_throughput and observed_throughput metrics per-tenant for a 30-day rolling window.
Credit ledger API (escrow_pool_balance, vesting_schedule, apply_credit) exists and is documented in the internal API spec.
Automation rules for Tier 1-3 remediation are implemented behind feature flags and have test coverage in staging.
Customer notification templates and appeal workflow are authored and approved by Legal and CS.
A sample contract clause is reviewed and signed-off by Legal and Finance or annotated with required changes.

End-to-end demo: simulate a sustained degradation incident in staging and show: detection -> automated remediation -> incident validation -> immediate credit issuance -> escrow vesting visible in ledger API.
